name: Practice With AI, Checks Without It
title: Practice With AI, Checks Without It
answer: Practice with AI, checks without it is a routine in which students use an AI tool for most of their practice and then sit a short assessment with no tool available, so the teacher can compare the two results. It matters because scores on practice can climb while genuine learning does not move, and students may not notice that the tool is doing the work for them.

sections.body: Scores on practice can climb while genuine learning does not move, so practice results alone cannot tell a teacher whether AI is helping. The idea answers that with a steady rhythm of checks taken without the tool, giving a second and independent signal of what a student can do unaided. It also covers a blind spot, since students may not recognise that leaning on the tool has cost them. Comparing the two sets of results for each student turns a vague worry into something visible and actionable. Where the two diverge, the response is a conversation rather than a verdict.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a mathematics class the pattern is practice with an adaptive program or tutor on most days, then a short quiz on paper each week. The teacher then compares the two results student by student. When practice scores are high and quiz scores are low, that gap is the signal that the student may be leaning on the tool, and it prompts a conversation. The chapter covers mathematics from kindergarten through twelfth grade, and the trials the text cites come from high school mathematics and a university programming course. Figure 7.4 sets out a simple weekly pattern for this rhythm.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not attach a formal evidence label to this idea; it reports findings from two trials. In a high school mathematics trial, practice scores rose while real learning stayed flat, and the same pattern appeared in a university programming course, where students who used AI scored better on exercises yet learned no more than students who went without it (Bassner et al., 2026). In that study the students also preferred the tool that helped them least. In the high school trial, students did not think copying answers had harmed them, although it had (Bastani et al., 2025). Figure 7.4 shows a simple weekly pattern.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about interpretation and about who decides. A low quiz score beside a high practice score is a signal, not proof, and the text's response is a conversation with the student rather than a conclusion about them. The teacher keeps the judgement about what the gap means and what to do next. Students cannot be left to assess their own use of the tool, because the high school trial showed they did not think copying answers had harmed them even when it had. The weekly check without AI is what gives students honest information about what they can do on their own, and holding to that check is a decision the school makes.
